<script type="application/json" id="pack-y2w09">{"year":2,"week":9,"id":"y2w09","title":"Data Collection Instruments","subtitle":"Designing, piloting and improving questionnaires, interview guides and observation guides; writing clear, unbiased questions and non-overlapping options; rating scales; choosing a fair sample; and judging an instrument for bias, language, gender, ethics, cost, time, privacy and cultural sensitivity, with digital tools where available.","family":"data","section":{"no":4,"name":"Data Collection, Organisation and Representation","strand":"Making Sense of and Using Data","from":9,"to":11},"outcomes":["Design a questionnaire, an interview guide and an observation guide for a real question.","Write clear closed, open and probing questions, with response options that do not overlap.","Code rating-scale answers and summarise them with frequencies, percentages and a mean score.","Choose a fair sample (random, systematic or stratified) and work out sample sizes.","Evaluate an instrument for bias, language, gender, ethics, cost, time, privacy and culture."],"keywords":["data collection instrument","questionnaire","interview guide","observation guide","checklist","closed question","open question","probing question","Likert scale","pilot test","population","sample","random sample","systematic sample","stratified sample","response rate","bias","leading question","double-barrelled","confidentiality","consent"],"notes":[{"title":"Why instruments matter","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **data collection instrument** is the tool you use to gather information: a questionnaire, an interview guide, an observation guide or a checklist. Good conclusions need good data, and good data needs a well-designed instrument. In Year 1 you met the main types of data; this week you design the tools yourself and judge their quality."},{"k":"fig","id":"w09-instruments","caption":"Three instruments and what each does best."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Types of data (review)","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Categorical** data are words or labels: **nominal** (no order, such as favourite subject) or **ordinal** (ordered, such as a rating from \"poor\" to \"excellent\").","**Numerical** data are numbers: **discrete** (counted, such as number of siblings) or **continuous** (measured, such as height).","**Quantitative** instruments collect numbers you can analyse; **qualitative** instruments collect words, opinions and descriptions."]}]}],"figs":["w09-instruments"]},{"title":"Designing a questionnaire","blocks":[{"k":"ol","items":["**Define the purpose.** What do you want to find out, and from whom (the **target group**)?","**Write the questions.** Use **closed questions** (fixed options: yes/no, multiple choice, rating scales) for counting, and a few **open questions** for detail.","**Organise it.** Begin with a short **introduction** stating the purpose and promising **confidentiality**. Put easy questions first and sensitive ones near the end. Keep it short: about 10–15 questions.","**Pilot test** it with a few people from the target group, and ask for feedback.","**Revise** and then **distribute** it, on paper or online, with clear instructions."]},{"k":"fig","id":"w09-cycle","caption":"The design cycle for any instrument."}],"figs":["w09-cycle"]},{"title":"Writing good questions","blocks":[{"k":"table","head":["Problem","Poor question","Better question"],"rows":[["leading","Don't you agree the canteen is too expensive?","How would you rate canteen prices? (very cheap … very expensive)"],["double-barrelled","Do you enjoy maths and science?","Do you enjoy maths? / Do you enjoy science?"],["vague","Do you study often?","How many hours do you study on a school day?"],["overlapping options","1–2 h, 2–3 h, 3–4 h","less than 2 h, 2 h to less than 3 h, 3 h or more"],["missing option","Bus or taxi?","Bus, taxi, walk, other (please state)"]]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Options must not overlap","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Response options must be **mutually exclusive** (no answer fits two boxes) and **exhaustive** (every answer fits a box). Add \"other (please specify)\" when you cannot list every choice."}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Rating scales","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **Likert scale** asks how strongly a person agrees with a statement. Each option is given a **code**, so the answers can be counted and averaged."},{"k":"fig","id":"w09-likert","caption":"A five-point rating scale and the results from 20 students."},{"k":"math","tex":"\\text{mean score}=\\frac{\\sum(\\text{code}\\times\\text{frequency})}{\\text{number of responses}}"},{"k":"p","text":"A mean above 3 shows overall agreement; below 3 shows overall disagreement."}],"figs":["w09-likert"]},{"title":"Interview guides","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"An **interview guide** is a planned list of questions for a spoken conversation."},{"k":"ul","items":["Start with an **icebreaker** and an introduction that explains the purpose and promises confidentiality.","Use **open questions** (\"Can you describe…?\") and **probing questions** (\"Can you tell me more about…?\").","Keep to about 8–12 questions; practise with a classmate first.","Record answers accurately (notes, or audio **with permission**)."]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Observation guides","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"An **observation guide** lists the behaviours to watch for, grouped into **categories**, with a **checklist** or **tally** to record how often each happens. It also states **where**, **when** and **for how long** you will observe, so that sessions can be compared fairly."},{"k":"table","head":["Category","Behaviour","Count"],"rows":[["active","raises hand","6"],["active","joins group discussion","7"],["passive","listens attentively","9"],["passive","takes notes","5"],["distraction","talks to classmates","3"],["distraction","uses phone","1"]]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Choosing who to ask: samples","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The **population** is everyone you want to know about; a **sample** is the part you actually ask. A sample must be **representative**, or the results are **biased**."},{"k":"ul","items":["**Simple random sample:** every member has an equal chance (draw names from a box, or use random numbers).","**Systematic sample:** choose every $k$-th person from a list, where $k=\\dfrac{\\text{population}}{\\text{sample size}}$, after a random start.","**Stratified sample:** split the population into groups (**strata**) and sample each group in proportion to its size."]},{"k":"fig","id":"w09-strata","caption":"A stratified sample keeps the same proportions as the population."},{"k":"math","tex":"\\text{stratum sample}=\\frac{\\text{stratum size}}{N}\\times n"},{"k":"p","text":"where $N$ is the population size and $n$ the sample size."},{"k":"p","text":"The **response rate** is $\\dfrac{\\text{number returned}}{\\text{number given out}}\\times100\\%$. A low response rate may make the results unreliable."}],"figs":["w09-strata"]},{"title":"Evaluating an instrument","blocks":[{"k":"table","head":["Issue","Ask yourself"],"rows":[["bias","Do the questions or the sample favour one answer or group?"],["language","Is the wording simple and clear to every respondent?"],["gender and culture","Is anything offensive, stereotyped or insensitive?"],["ethics and consent","Do people know the purpose and agree to take part?"],["privacy","Are names needed? Will answers be kept confidential?"],["cost and time","Can you afford to print it? How long does it take?"]]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Digital tools","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Instruments can be typed in a word processor, set out in a spreadsheet, or built as an **online form** (such as Google Forms or Microsoft Forms). Online forms collect answers straight into a spreadsheet, where functions such as `COUNTIF` tally them. But only people with phones or internet can reply, which can bias the sample (the **digital divide**)."}],"figs":[]}],"examples":[{"title":"Classifying questions and data","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"For each question, say whether it is open or closed and what type of data it gives. (a) How many people live in your house? (b) What is your favourite subject? (c) Rate the canteen food from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent). (d) What would make school sports better?"}],"steps":["(a) Closed; numerical, **discrete** (it is counted).","(b) Closed (with options); categorical, **nominal** (no order).","(c) Closed; categorical, **ordinal** (the ratings are ordered).","(d) Open; qualitative (words and ideas)."],"answer":"(a) discrete (b) nominal (c) ordinal (d) open, qualitative","figs":[]},{"title":"Improving poor questions","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Explain what is wrong with each question and rewrite it. (a) \"Don't you think our school needs a new library?\" (b) \"How old are you? 12–14, 14–16, 16–18\" (c) \"Do you like reading novels and newspapers?\""}],"steps":["(a) **Leading**: it pushes the respondent towards \"yes\". Better: \"How satisfied are you with the school library? (very satisfied, satisfied, unsure, dissatisfied, very dissatisfied)\".","(b) **Overlapping** and incomplete: a 14-year-old fits two boxes, and anyone over 18 fits none. Better: \"12–13, 14–15, 16–17, 18 or older\".","(c) **Double-barrelled**: a person may like one but not the other. Ask two separate questions."],"answer":"(a) leading (b) overlapping options (c) double-barrelled","figs":[]},{"title":"Summarising a rating scale","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Twenty students responded to \"Mathematics is useful in daily life\": strongly agree 8, agree 6, neutral 3, disagree 2, strongly disagree 1. Using codes 5 to 1, find the mean score and the percentage who agree or strongly agree."}],"steps":["$\\sum(\\text{code}\\times f)=5(8)+4(6)+3(3)+2(2)+1(1)=40+24+9+4+1=78$.","Mean score $=\\dfrac{78}{20}=3.9$.","Agree or strongly agree: $8+6=14$ out of 20, that is $\\dfrac{14}{20}\\times100\\%=70\\%$.","A mean of 3.9 (above the neutral 3) shows that most students agree."],"answer":"Mean score 3.9; 70% agree","figs":[]},{"title":"A stratified sample","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A school has 600 students: 240 in Form 1, 200 in Form 2 and 160 in Form 3. A stratified sample of 60 is needed. How many should be chosen from each form?"}],"steps":["Form 1: $\\dfrac{240}{600}\\times60=24$.","Form 2: $\\dfrac{200}{600}\\times60=20$.","Form 3: $\\dfrac{160}{600}\\times60=16$.","Check: $24+20+16=60$ ✓."],"answer":"24, 20 and 16","figs":[]},{"title":"A systematic sample","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"From a register of 600 students, a systematic sample of 60 is needed. The random start is 7. Which numbers are chosen, and what is the 20th student chosen?"}],"steps":["Interval $k=\\dfrac{600}{60}=10$: choose every 10th student.","Starting at 7: 7, 17, 27, 37, …, 597.","The $n$th number is $7+10(n-1)$, so the 20th is $7+10(19)=197$."],"answer":"7, 17, 27, …, 597; the 20th is number 197","figs":[]},{"title":"From checklist to percentages","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"An observation of 10 students in a maths lesson recorded: raised hand 6, joined group discussion 7, listened attentively 9, took notes 5, talked to classmates 3, used a phone 1. Express each as a percentage and comment."}],"steps":["Each student is $10\\%$ of the group: 60%, 70%, 90%, 50%, 30% and 10%.","Most students listened (90%) and joined the group work (70%), but only half took notes.","Distraction was low: 30% talked and 10% used a phone."],"answer":"60%, 70%, 90%, 50%, 30%, 10%","figs":[]},{"title":"Response rate and cost","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"150 questionnaires of 3 pages each were printed at GH₵0.50 a page; 117 were returned. Find (a) the printing cost (b) the response rate (c) the cost per returned questionnaire."}],"steps":["(a) Pages $=150\\times3=450$; cost $=450\\times0.50=$ GH₵225.","(b) Response rate $=\\dfrac{117}{150}\\times100\\%=78\\%$.","(c) $\\dfrac{225}{117}\\approx$ GH₵1.92 per returned questionnaire."],"answer":"(a) GH₵225 (b) 78% (c) about GH₵1.92","figs":[]},{"title":"Evaluating an instrument","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A teacher hands out a questionnaire in class asking students to write their **name** and answer \"How many times have you smoked this month?\". Evaluate this instrument and suggest improvements."}],"steps":["**Privacy and honesty:** asking for names on a sensitive question will make students hide the truth. Make it anonymous.","**Bias:** the teacher's presence may pressure students. Use a sealed box for returns, collected by someone else.","**Ethics:** state the purpose, ask for consent, and allow students to skip the question.","**Order:** put the sensitive question near the end, after easier questions."],"answer":"Remove names, ensure confidentiality and consent, reduce pressure, reorder questions","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Data collection instruments","items":["Design cycle: purpose → questions → organise → pilot → revise → collect.","Questions must be clear, neutral, single-issue; options must not overlap and must cover every case.","Likert mean score $=\\dfrac{\\sum(\\text{code}\\times f)}{n}$.","Systematic interval $k=\\dfrac{N}{n}$; stratum sample $=\\dfrac{\\text{stratum}}{N}\\times n$.","Response rate $=\\dfrac{\\text{returned}}{\\text{given out}}\\times100\\%$.","Check every instrument for bias, language, gender, ethics, privacy, culture, cost and time."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"Which question is **closed**?","options":["Do you walk to school? (yes / no)","Why do you enjoy football?","Describe your journey to school.","What would improve the canteen?"],"correct":0,"explain":"It has fixed answer options."},{"q":"\"Number of siblings\" gives data that are","options":["numerical and discrete","numerical and continuous","categorical and nominal","categorical and ordinal"],"correct":0,"explain":"Siblings are counted."},{"q":"\"Don't you agree that homework is too much?\" is","options":["a leading question","a double-barrelled question","an open question","a neutral question"],"correct":0,"explain":"It suggests the expected answer."},{"q":"Which set of options is correct for daily study time?","options":["less than 1 h; 1 h to less than 2 h; 2 h or more","0–1 h; 1–2 h; 2–3 h","1–2 h; 3–4 h","a little; a lot"],"correct":0,"explain":"The options do not overlap and cover every case."},{"q":"The first step in designing any instrument is to","options":["define its purpose and target group","print the questions","pilot test it","analyse the results"],"correct":0,"explain":"Everything else follows from the purpose."},{"q":"Responses coded 5, 4, 4, 3 and 4 have mean score","options":["4","3","4.5","20"],"correct":0,"explain":"$20\\div5=4$."},{"q":"A population of 800 and a systematic sample of 40 give an interval of","options":["20","40","32","5"],"correct":0,"explain":"$800\\div40=20$."},{"q":"A class of 30 has 18 girls. In a stratified sample of 10 from the class, the number of girls is","options":["6","4","9","3"],"correct":0,"explain":"$\\tfrac{18}{30}\\times10=6$."},{"q":"90 questionnaires were given out and 63 returned. The response rate is","options":["70%","63%","27%","143%"],"correct":0,"explain":"$\\tfrac{63}{90}=0.7$."},{"q":"Why is a pilot test carried out?","options":["to find unclear questions before the real survey","to collect the final data","to make the questionnaire longer","to choose the sample"],"correct":0,"explain":"Feedback from the pilot is used to revise the instrument."}],"exercise":[{"q":"State the type of data from: (a) height in cm (b) shoe size (c) favourite colour (d) rating of a film from 1 to 5.","a":"(a) continuous (b) discrete (c) nominal (d) ordinal"},{"q":"What is wrong with \"Don't you think the new uniform is too expensive?\" Rewrite it.","a":"Leading. \"How would you describe the price of the new uniform? (very cheap, cheap, fair, expensive, very expensive)\""},{"q":"What is wrong with \"How often do you use the library and the computer lab?\"","a":"Double-barrelled: ask about each place separately"},{"q":"Fix the age options 13–15, 15–17, 17–19.","a":"Overlapping and incomplete: 13–14, 15–16, 17–18, 19 or older"},{"q":"A school has 360 Science, 270 Business and 270 Arts students. Find a stratified sample of 50.","a":"$20$, $15$ and $15$"},{"q":"A systematic sample of 40 is taken from a list of 400 with random start 3. List the first four numbers and find the 15th.","a":"3, 13, 23, 33; the 15th is $3+14\\times10=143$"},{"q":"80 questionnaires were given out and 52 returned. Find the response rate.","a":"65%"},{"q":"A rating scale gave: SA 5, A 10, N 6, D 3, SD 1. Find the mean score (codes 5 to 1).","a":"$\\tfrac{25+40+18+6+1}{25}=\\tfrac{90}{25}=3.6$"},{"q":"A 2-page questionnaire is printed for 120 respondents at GH₵0.40 a page. What percentage is this?","a":"75%"}],"theory":[{"q":"Explain briefly how each of these can be designed: (a) a questionnaire (b) an interview guide (c) an observation guide.","steps":["(a) **Questionnaire:** state the purpose and target group; write mostly closed questions with clear, non-overlapping options and a few open questions; add an introduction that promises confidentiality; order from easy to sensitive; keep to about 10–15 questions; pilot test, revise, then distribute.","(b) **Interview guide:** state the purpose and who will be interviewed; write an icebreaker, open questions and probing follow-ups; order from general to specific; keep to about 8–12 questions; practise with a mock interview; record answers accurately with permission.","(c) **Observation guide:** state the purpose and the setting; list the behaviours to observe, grouped into categories; make a checklist or tally sheet; fix the times and length of each observation so sessions can be compared."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"Design a short questionnaire (introduction and six questions) to find out how students feel about the school canteen.","steps":["**Introduction:** \"We are surveying students to help improve the canteen. Your answers are anonymous and will be kept confidential. Thank you.\"","Which form are you in? ☐ Form 1 ☐ Form 2 ☐ Form 3","How many days a week do you buy food at the canteen? ☐ 0 ☐ 1–2 ☐ 3–4 ☐ 5","How would you rate the taste of the food? ☐ very poor ☐ poor ☐ fair ☐ good ☐ very good","How would you describe the prices? ☐ very cheap ☐ cheap ☐ fair ☐ expensive ☐ very expensive","How clean is the eating area? (rate 1 = very dirty to 5 = very clean) ☐1 ☐2 ☐3 ☐4 ☐5","What one change would most improve the canteen? ____________","The options in each closed question do not overlap and cover every case; question 6 is open for detail."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"You piloted a questionnaire with four respondents. State three things you could do when reviewing it, giving a reason for each.","steps":["**Reword unclear questions** that the respondents asked about or misread, so that every person understands them the same way.","**Fix answer options** where a respondent's answer did not fit or fitted two boxes, so the options are exhaustive and mutually exclusive.","**Time it and shorten it** if it took too long, so that real respondents do not give up halfway; remove questions that do not serve the purpose.","Others: reorder questions so sensitive ones come last; remove leading or offensive wording; check that the answers can actually be analysed."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"A club wants to know how much pocket money students in a school of 1200 receive. It sends an online form through the club's WhatsApp group. Evaluate this plan for bias, privacy and ethics, and propose a better plan.","steps":["**Bias:** only club members, and only those with phones, will reply. They may not represent the whole school (sampling bias and the digital divide).","**Privacy and ethics:** pocket money is personal. Names or phone numbers linked to answers could embarrass students. Respondents should know the purpose and agree to take part.","**Better plan:** take a **stratified random sample** (for example 60 students in proportion to each form), use an **anonymous** paper or online questionnaire, give **ranges** of amounts rather than exact figures, explain the purpose and ask for consent, and collect replies in a sealed box."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"Compare a paper questionnaire with an online form for collecting data from 300 students. Include cost, time, accuracy and fairness.","steps":["**Paper:** costs money for printing (for example 300 copies × 2 pages × GH₵0.40 = GH₵240) and takes time to hand out, collect and type up; typing can introduce errors; but every student can take part.","**Online form:** almost free; answers go straight into a spreadsheet, where `COUNTIF` and charts summarise them quickly and without copying errors; but only students with a phone or internet can respond, which may bias the results.","A mixed approach (online for those with access, paper for the rest) keeps the speed and stays fair."],"answer":"","model":null}],"checklist":["I can design a questionnaire, an interview guide and an observation guide.","I can write clear, neutral questions with non-overlapping options.","I can <script type="application/json" id="pack-y2w10">{"year":2,"week":10,"id":"y2w10","title":"Data Representation: Ogives, Waffle Charts and Box Plots","subtitle":"Cumulative frequency tables and less-than and greater-than ogives; reading the median, quartiles and percentiles from an ogive and by interpolation; waffle charts for parts of a whole; five-number summaries, box-and-whisker plots and outliers; comparing distributions; 3D charts; and a data mini-project.","family":"data","section":{"no":4,"name":"Data Collection, Organisation and Representation","strand":"Making Sense of and Using Data","from":9,"to":11},"outcomes":["Build cumulative frequency tables and draw less-than and greater-than ogives.","Estimate the median, quartiles, interquartile range and percentiles from an ogive, and check them by interpolation.","Represent parts of a whole with a waffle chart.","Find a five-number summary, draw a box plot and identify outliers.","Compare distributions with box plots and judge when a 3D chart helps or misleads."],"keywords":["cumulative frequency","ogive","less-than ogive","greater-than ogive","upper class boundary","median","quartile","interquartile range","percentile","interpolation","waffle chart","five-number summary","box-and-whisker plot","whisker","outlier","distribution","3D chart"],"notes":[{"title":"Organising data","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Raw data become useful when they are **organised** in a table and **represented** in a diagram. In Year 1 you used bar charts, pie charts and histograms. This week adds diagrams that show how data **accumulate** and how they **spread**."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Cumulative frequency","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The **cumulative frequency** of a class is the running total of the frequencies up to and including that class. The last cumulative frequency equals the total, $n$."},{"k":"table","head":["Class","0–20","20–40","40–60","60–80","80–100"],"rows":[["Frequency","4","6","5","3","2"],["Cumulative frequency","4","10","15","18","20"]]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"The ogive (cumulative frequency curve)","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Drawing a less-than ogive","blocks":[{"k":"ol","items":["Make a cumulative frequency table.","Plot each cumulative frequency against the **upper class boundary** of its class.","Start the curve at the lower boundary of the first class, with cumulative frequency 0.","Join the points with a smooth curve."]}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w10-ogive1","caption":"A less-than ogive; reading across from $\\tfrac n2$ gives the median."},{"k":"p","text":"A **greater-than ogive** shows how many values are **at least** each lower class boundary. Work the running totals from the **top class down**, and plot them against the **lower class boundaries**. The curve falls. The less-than and greater-than ogives **cross at the median**."}],"figs":["w10-ogive1"]},{"title":"Reading an ogive","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"For $n$ values:"},{"k":"table","head":["Measure","Read across from"],"rows":[["lower quartile $Q_1$","$\\tfrac14n$"],["median $Q_2$","$\\tfrac12n$"],["upper quartile $Q_3$","$\\tfrac34n$"],["$p$th percentile","$\\tfrac{p}{100}n$"]]},{"k":"p","text":"The **interquartile range** $\\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1$ measures the spread of the middle half of the data."},{"k":"fig","id":"w10-heights","caption":"Reading the quartiles of 50 heights from an ogive."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Median by interpolation","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"For grouped data, the median can be calculated instead of read:"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\text{median}=L+\\left(\\frac{\\tfrac n2-F}{f}\\right)\\times c"},{"k":"p","text":"where $L$ is the lower boundary of the median class, $F$ the cumulative frequency before it, $f$ its frequency and $c$ its width. The same formula with $\\tfrac n4$ or $\\tfrac{3n}{4}$ gives $Q_1$ or $Q_3$."}]}],"figs":["w10-heights"]},{"title":"Waffle charts","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **waffle chart** is a $10\\times10$ grid of 100 squares. Each square stands for **1%** (or a fixed number of items), and each category gets its own colour."},{"k":"fig","id":"w10-waffle","caption":"Each square is one student out of 100."},{"k":"p","text":"To draw one: convert each category to a percentage, colour that many squares, and add a key. Waffle charts make parts of a whole easier to compare than the angles of a pie chart."}],"figs":["w10-waffle"]},{"title":"Box-and-whisker plots","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **box plot** shows the **five-number summary**: minimum, $Q_1$, median, $Q_3$ and maximum."},{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Quartiles of a list","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Arrange the data in order. The **median** is the middle value (the mean of the two middle values if $n$ is even). $Q_1$ is the median of the lower half and $Q_3$ the median of the upper half; if $n$ is odd, leave the overall median out of both halves."}]},{"k":"ul","items":["The **box** runs from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$ and holds the middle 50% of the data; a line marks the median.","The **whiskers** run from the box to the minimum and the maximum.","Each of the four sections holds about a **quarter** of the data."]},{"k":"fig","id":"w10-dice","caption":"Box plot of 20 dice throws."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Outliers","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A value is an **outlier** if it is below $Q_1-1.5\\times\\text{IQR}$ or above $Q_3+1.5\\times\\text{IQR}$. Outliers can be marked with a cross and the whisker stopped at the most extreme value that is not an outlier."}]}],"figs":["w10-dice"]},{"title":"Comparing distributions","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"To compare two sets of data with box plots, comment on **average** (compare the medians) and **spread** (compare the IQRs and ranges), in the context of the question."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"3D charts","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Spreadsheets can draw bar and pie charts in **3D**. They look attractive, but the depth and perspective make heights and angles harder to read, and the front of a 3D pie looks bigger than it is. Use 3D charts for display, and 2D charts when accurate reading matters."},{"k":"fig","id":"w10-3d","caption":"A 3D column chart: attractive, but harder to read exactly."}],"figs":["w10-3d"]}],"examples":[{"title":"A less-than ogive","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Draw an ogive for the distribution below and use it to estimate the median."},{"k":"table","head":["Class","Frequency"],"rows":[["0–20","4"],["20–40","6"],["40–60","5"],["60–80","3"],["80–100","2"]]}],"steps":["Cumulative frequencies: 4, 10, 15, 18, 20.","Plot $(0,0)$, $(20,4)$, $(40,10)$, $(60,15)$, $(80,18)$, $(100,20)$ and join with a smooth curve (see the figure in the notes).","$\\tfrac n2=10$. Reading across from 10 and down gives the median 40.","Check by interpolation: median class 20–40, $\\ 20+\\dfrac{10-4}{6}\\times20=40$ ✓."],"answer":"Median $=40$","figs":[]},{"title":"Quartiles from an ogive","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The heights of 50 students are given below. <script type="application/json" id="pack-y2w11">{"year":2,"week":11,"id":"y2w11","title":"Measures of Dispersion: Analysing and Interpreting Data","subtitle":"Why averages are not enough; range, interquartile range and quartile deviation; mean absolute deviation; variance and standard deviation for a population and a sample, for lists and frequency tables; interpreting spread in real contexts; and choosing the measure that best suits the data.","family":"data","section":{"no":4,"name":"Data Collection, Organisation and Representation","strand":"Making Sense of and Using Data","from":9,"to":11},"outcomes":["Explain what dispersion means and why two data sets with the same mean can differ.","Calculate the range, interquartile range and quartile deviation.","Calculate the mean absolute deviation, variance and standard deviation of a list or a frequency table.","Distinguish population and sample variance, and interpret a standard deviation in context.","Justify which measure of spread best suits a given data set."],"keywords":["dispersion","spread","variability","range","quartile","interquartile range","quartile deviation","semi-interquartile range","deviation","mean absolute deviation","variance","standard deviation","population","sample","frequency table","consistent","outlier","robust"],"notes":[{"title":"Why spread matters","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"An average tells you the centre of the data; a **measure of dispersion** tells you how **spread out** the data are. Two classes can have the same mean mark, yet one may have every student close to the mean while the other has some very high and some very low marks."},{"k":"fig","id":"w11-dots","caption":"Same mean and range, very different spread."}],"figs":["w11-dots"]},{"title":"Range","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"\\text{range}=\\text{maximum}-\\text{minimum}"},{"k":"p","text":"The range is quick to find, but it uses only two values, so a single extreme value can change it a lot, and it says nothing about the values in between."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Interquartile range and quartile deviation","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"\\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1\\qquad\\text{quartile deviation}=\\frac{Q_3-Q_1}{2}"},{"k":"p","text":"The **interquartile range** is the spread of the middle 50% of the data. The **quartile deviation** (semi-interquartile range) is half of it. Both ignore the extreme values, so they are **robust**: outliers hardly affect them. Use them with the **median**."},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"Finding quartiles of a list","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Order the data. The median splits it into two halves (leave the median out of both halves if $n$ is odd). $Q_1$ is the median of the lower half, $Q_3$ the median of the upper half."}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Deviations from the mean","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The **deviation** of a value $x$ is $x-\\bar x$: how far it is above (positive) or below (negative) the mean."},{"k":"fig","id":"w11-dev","caption":"Deviations of 3, 4, 7, 12 and 14 from their mean 8."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"The deviations always add up to zero","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"$\\sum(x-\\bar x)=\\sum x-n\\bar x=n\\bar x-n\\bar x=0$. So the plain average of the deviations is useless as a measure of spread. We remove the signs either with **absolute values** (mean absolute deviation) or by **squaring** (variance)."}]}],"figs":["w11-dev"]},{"title":"Mean absolute deviation","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"\\text{MAD}=\\frac{\\sum|x-\\bar x|}{n}"},{"k":"p","text":"The MAD is the average distance of the values from the mean. It is easy to understand, in the same units as the data."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Variance and standard deviation","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Variance and standard deviation","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"For a **population** of $n$ values:"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\sigma^2=\\frac{\\sum(x-\\bar x)^2}{n}\\qquad\\sigma=\\sqrt{\\frac{\\sum(x-\\bar x)^2}{n}}"},{"k":"p","text":"For a **sample** used to estimate a population, divide by $n-1$:"},{"k":"math","tex":"s^2=\\frac{\\sum(x-\\bar x)^2}{n-1}"}]},{"k":"p","text":"**Steps:** find the mean; subtract it from each value; square each deviation; add the squares; divide by $n$ (or $n-1$); take the square root for the standard deviation."},{"k":"p","text":"The **standard deviation** (SD) is in the same units as the data, so it is the most used measure of spread. A **small** SD means the values are **close to the mean** (consistent); a **large** SD means they are **widely spread**."},{"k":"fig","id":"w11-band","caption":"Values within one standard deviation of the mean."}],"figs":["w11-band"]},{"title":"Frequency tables","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"When each value $x$ occurs $f$ times, use the frequencies (for grouped data, $x$ is the **class midpoint**):"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\bar x=\\frac{\\sum fx}{\\sum f}\\qquad\\sigma^2=\\frac{\\sum f(x-\\bar x)^2}{\\sum f}=\\frac{\\sum fx^2}{\\sum f}-\\bar x^2"},{"k":"p","text":"The second form is quicker: find $\\sum fx^2$, divide by $\\sum f$, then subtract the square of the mean."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Changing the data","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["Adding the same number to every value moves the mean but **does not change** the spread.","Multiplying every value by $k$ multiplies the mean, range, IQR and SD by $|k|$, and the variance by $k^2$."]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Choosing a measure","blocks":[{"k":"fig","id":"w11-choose","caption":"Choose the measure of spread to suit the data."},{"k":"table","head":["Measure","Strength","Weakness"],"rows":[["range","very quick","uses only two values; affected by outliers"],["IQR / QD","not affected by outliers","ignores half the data"],["MAD","easy to understand","harder to use in further work"],["SD / variance","uses every value","affected by outliers; variance is in squared units"]]}],"figs":["w11-choose"]}],"examples":[{"title":"The range in context","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The mathematics test scores of 10 students are 45, 78, 56, 89, 92, 67, 81, 74, 58 and 62. Find the range and explain what it tells the teacher."}],"steps":["Highest score 92, lowest score 45.","Range $=92-45=47$.","There is a 47-mark gap between the strongest and weakest student: performance varies widely, so some students may need extra support.","The range uses only two scores, so the teacher should also look at a measure that uses all the scores."],"answer":"Range $=47$","figs":[]},{"title":"Interquartile range and quartile deviation","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Find the IQR and quartile deviation of the test scores 56, 61, 63, 68, 70, 71, 73, 75, 78, 80, 85."}],"steps":["The data are in order and $n=11$, so the median is the 6th value, 71.","Lower half: 56, 61, 63, 68, 70, so $Q_1=63$. Upper half: 73, 75, 78, 80, 85, so $Q_3=78$.","IQR $=78-63=15$; quartile deviation $=\\dfrac{15}{2}=7.5$.","The middle half of the scores lie within a 15-mark band around the median."],"answer":"IQR $=15$, QD $=7.5$","figs":[]},{"title":"Mean absolute deviation","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Five test scores are 85, 90, 88, 92, 87. Find the mean absolute deviation."}],"steps":["Mean $=\\dfrac{442}{5}=88.4$.","Absolute deviations: $3.4,\\ 1.6,\\ 0.4,\\ 3.6,\\ 1.4$.","MAD $=\\dfrac{3.4+1.6+0.4+3.6+1.4}{5}=\\dfrac{10.4}{5}=2.08$.","On average a score is about 2 marks from the mean: the scores are very consistent."],"answer":"MAD $=2.08$","figs":[]},{"title":"Population variance and SD","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Find the variance and standard deviation of the population $\\{3,\\ 5,\\ 8,\\ 1\\}$."}],"steps":["Mean $=\\dfrac{17}{4}=4.25$.","Deviations: $-1.25,\\ 0.75,\\ 3.75,\\ -3.25$ (they add to 0 ✓).","Squares: $1.5625,\\ 0.5625,\\ 14.0625,\\ 10.5625$; sum $=26.75$.","$\\sigma^2=\\dfrac{26.75}{4}\\approx6.69$ and $\\sigma=\\sqrt{6.6875}\\approx2.59$."],"answer":"Variance $\\approx6.69$, SD $\\approx2.59$","figs":[]},{"title":"Sample variance","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The values 3, 4, 7, 12, 14 are a sample. Find the sample variance and standard deviation."}],"steps":["Mean $=\\dfrac{40}{5}=8$; deviations $-5,\\ -4,\\ -1,\\ 4,\\ 6$ (see the figure in the notes).","Sum of squares $=25+16+1+16+36=94$.","Sample: divide by $n-1=4$: $\\ s^2=\\dfrac{94}{4}=23.5$.","$s=\\sqrt{23.5}\\approx4.85$."],"answer":"$s^2=23.5$, $s\\approx4.85$","figs":[]},{"title":"Interpreting a standard deviation","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The annual salaries (GH₵ thousands) of 10 employees are 45, 52, 47, 49, 50, 60, 55, 53, 58, 62. Find the mean and standard deviation and interpret them."}],"steps":["Mean $=\\dfrac{531}{10}=53.1$, that is GH₵53 100.","Squared deviations: 65.61, 1.21, 37.21, 16.81, 9.61, 47.61, 3.61, 0.01, 24.01, 79.21; sum $=284.9$.","$\\sigma=\\sqrt{\\dfrac{284.9}{10}}=\\sqrt{28.49}\\approx5.34$, that is about GH₵5340.","A typical salary is about GH₵5300 from the mean; 6 of the 10 salaries lie within one SD (see the figure in the notes). The spread is moderate, so pay is fairly even."],"answer":"Mean GH₵53 100; SD $\\approx$ GH₵5340","figs":[]},{"title":"Standard deviation from grouped data","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The masses of 20 bags of rice are shown. Estimate the mean and standard deviation."},{"k":"table","head":["Mass (kg)","Frequency"],"rows":[["40–50","4"],["50–60","10"],["60–70","4"],["70–80","2"]]}],"steps":["Midpoints $x$: 45, 55, 65, 75. $\\ \\sum fx=180+550+260+150=1140$, so $\\bar x=\\dfrac{1140}{20}=57$ kg.","$\\sum fx^2=4(2025)+10(3025)+4(4225)+2(5625)=66\\,500$.","$\\sigma^2=\\dfrac{66\\,500}{20}-57^2=3325-3249=76$.","$\\sigma=\\sqrt{76}\\approx8.72$ kg. (These are estimates, because midpoints stand in for the actual masses.)"],"answer":"Mean $\\approx57$ kg, SD $\\approx8.72$ kg","figs":[]},{"title":"Comparing consistency","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Kofi's goals in five matches are 12, 15, 18, 15, 15 and Yaw's are 5, 25, 10, 20, 15. Compare them."}],"steps":["Both means are $\\dfrac{75}{5}=15$.","Kofi: squared deviations $9+0+9+0+0=18$, $\\ \\sigma=\\sqrt{3.6}\\approx1.90$.","Yaw: $100+100+25+25+0=250$, $\\ \\sigma=\\sqrt{50}\\approx7.07$.","Same average, but Kofi's much smaller SD shows he is far more **consistent**; Yaw is unpredictable."],"answer":"Equal means; Kofi is more consistent (SD 1.90 against 7.07).","figs":[]},{"title":"Choosing the best measure","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The monthly incomes (GH₵) of seven workers are 900, 950, 1000, 1000, 1100, 1200, 9500. Which average and which measure of spread best describe the data? Justify your choice."}],"steps":["The value 9500 is an outlier: $Q_1=950$, $Q_3=1200$, IQR $=250$, upper fence $1200+375=1575$.","Range $=8600$ and the SD (about 2970) are both inflated by that one value; the mean ($\\approx2236$) is higher than six of the seven incomes.","The **median** (1000) with the **IQR** (250) or QD (125) describes a typical worker much better, because they are not affected by the outlier."],"answer":"Median 1000 with IQR 250 (or QD 125)","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Measures of dispersion","items":["Range $=$ max $-$ min. IQR $=Q_3-Q_1$. QD $=\\tfrac12(Q_3-Q_1)$.","MAD $=\\dfrac{\\sum|x-\\bar x|}{n}$.","Population: $\\sigma^2=\\dfrac{\\sum(x-\\bar x)^2}{n}$; sample: $s^2=\\dfrac{\\sum(x-\\bar x)^2}{n-1}$; SD is the square root.","Frequency table: $\\sigma^2=\\dfrac{\\sum fx^2}{\\sum f}-\\bar x^2$.","Small SD: consistent data; large SD: widely spread.","Outliers or skew: median with IQR. Symmetric: mean with SD."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"The range of 60, 65, 70, 12, 52, 40, 48 is","options":["58","30","70","52"],"correct":0,"explain":"$70-12$."},{"q":"$Q_1=63$ and $Q_3=78$. The quartile deviation is","options":["7.5","15","70.5","141"],"correct":0,"explain":"$\\tfrac{78-63}{2}$."},{"q":"The sum of the deviations from the mean is always","options":["0","1","$n$","the variance"],"correct":0,"explain":"Positive and negative deviations cancel."},{"q":"The values 2, 4, 6 have mean absolute deviation","options":["$\\tfrac43$","2","4","$\\tfrac83$"],"correct":0,"explain":"Deviations 2, 0, 2; mean $\\tfrac43$."},{"q":"The population variance of 2, 4, 6 is","options":["$\\tfrac83$","4","$\\tfrac43$","8"],"correct":0,"explain":"Squares 4, 0, 4; $\\tfrac83$."},{"q":"A variance of 25 cm² gives a standard deviation of","options":["5 cm","12.5 cm","625 cm","25 cm"],"correct":0,"explain":"Square root."},{"q":"Sample variance divides the sum of squared deviations by","options":["$n-1$","$n$","$n+1$","$n^2$"],"correct":0,"explain":"This gives a better estimate of the population variance."},{"q":"Every value in a data set is increased by 10. The standard deviation","options":["stays the same","increases by 10","is multiplied by 10","increases by 100"],"correct":0,"explain":"Shifting all values does not change their spread."},{"q":"Two players have the same mean score; A has SD 2 and B has SD 9. (a) Find the mean. (b) Find the standard deviation. (c) Explain what the standard deviation says about the sales.","steps":["(a) $\\sum x=643$, so $\\bar x=\\dfrac{643}{12}\\approx53.58$, about GH₵53 580 a month.","(b) $\\sum(x-\\bar x)^2\\approx308.92$, so $\\sigma=\\sqrt{\\dfrac{308.92}{12}}\\approx\\sqrt{25.74}\\approx5.07$ (thousand).","(c) Monthly sales typically differ from the average by about GH₵5000, roughly 9% of the mean. Sales are fairly steady, so the owner can plan stock and staffing with some confidence, while allowing for months about GH₵5000 above or below average."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"The times (minutes) 8 people spent exercising in a week were 30, 45, 50, 35, 40, 55, 60, 50. Find the mean and the variance, and explain what the variance shows.","steps":["Mean $=\\dfrac{365}{8}=45.625$ min.","Squared deviations add to $721.875$, so $\\sigma^2=\\dfrac{721.875}{8}\\approx90.23$ min², and $\\sigma\\approx9.50$ min.","The variance is in **squared** minutes, so it is hard to picture; its square root, about 9.5 minutes, shows that a typical person's exercise time is about 9–10 minutes away from the mean. The group is moderately spread, from 30 to 60 minutes."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"Prove that $\\sum(x-\\bar x)=0$ for any data set, and explain why this means we square the deviations when measuring spread.","steps":["Since $\\bar x=\\dfrac{\\sum x}{n}$, we have $\\sum x=n\\bar x$. Then $\\sum(x-\\bar x)=\\sum x-n\\bar x=n\\bar x-n\\bar x=0.$","Values above the mean give positive deviations and values below give negative ones, and these always cancel exactly. The average deviation would be 0 for every data set, so it measures nothing. Squaring makes every term positive (and gives extra weight to values far from the mean); taking the square root at the end returns to the original units."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"Show that adding a constant $a$ to every value does not change the standard deviation, but multiplying every value by $k$ multiplies it by $|k|$. Hence convert temperatures with mean 30 °C and SD 1.6 °C to °F using $F=1.8C+32$.","steps":["**Adding $a$:** the mean becomes $\\bar x+a$, so each deviation $(x+a)-(\\bar x+a)=x-\\bar x$ is unchanged, and so is the SD.","**Multiplying by $k$:** the mean becomes $k\\bar x$, each deviation becomes $k(x-\\bar x)$, each squared deviation is multiplied by $k^2$, so the variance is multiplied by $k^2$ and the SD by $|k|$.","For $F=1.8C+32$: mean $=1.8(30)+32=86$ °F; SD $=1.8\\times1.6=2.88$ °F (adding 32 has no effect on the SD)."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"Two machines fill bags of sugar labelled 1 kg. overfills slightly on average, but its SD is only 0.01 kg, so nearly every bag is between about 1.00 and 1.04 kg: it is far more **consistent**, and customers always get at least 1 kg.","Machine B is <script type="application/json" id="pack-y2w12">{"year":2,"week":12,"id":"y2w12","title":"Ratios, Rates and Proportions","subtitle":"Part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios; simplifying and comparing ratios; sharing in a ratio with tape diagrams, ratio tables and algebra; combining ratios; rates and unit rates, best buys and unit conversions; proportion as an equation of two ratios; direct and inverse proportion; scales, models and exchange rates.","family":"number","section":{"no":5,"name":"Ratios, Rates and Proportions","strand":"Number for Everyday Life","from":12,"to":14},"outcomes":["Explain ratio and rate as ways of comparing quantities, and tell part-to-part from part-to-whole ratios.","Simplify ratios, write them in the form $1:n$, and combine two ratios into one.","Share a quantity in a given ratio by several methods.","Calculate unit rates, compare best buys and convert units of a rate.","Set up and solve proportions, and recognise direct and inverse proportion."],"keywords":["ratio","part-to-part","part-to-whole","simplest form","equivalent ratio","unitary method","tape diagram","ratio table","double number line","rate","unit rate","best buy","proportion","cross-multiplication","direct proportion","inverse proportion","constant of proportionality","scale","exchange rate"],"notes":[{"title":"Ratio","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **ratio** compares two or more quantities **of the same kind**, measured in the **same units**. The ratio of $a$ to $b$ is written $a:b$ or $\\dfrac ab$ and read \"$a$ to $b$\"."},{"k":"fig","id":"w12-parts","caption":"Part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios."},{"k":"ul","items":["A **part-to-part** ratio compares one part with another: red beads to blue beads, $3:5$.","A **part-to-whole** ratio compares one part with the total: red beads to all beads, $3:8$. It can be written as a fraction ($\\tfrac38$) or a percentage ($37.5\\%$)."]},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Simplifying ratios","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["Change both quantities to the **same units** first: $50\\text{ cm}:2\\text{ m}=50:200=1:4$.","Divide every part by the HCF: $30:20=3:2$.","Clear fractions or decimals by multiplying: $1.5:2=3:4$ and $\\tfrac12:\\tfrac13=3:2$.","The **form $1:n$** divides by the first part: $4:10=1:2.5$."]}]}],"figs":["w12-parts"]},{"title":"Sharing in a ratio","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"To share a quantity in the ratio $a:b$, there are $a+b$ equal **parts** in total."},{"k":"fig","id":"w12-tape","caption":"Sharing 30 in the ratio $2:3$ with a tape diagram."},{"k":"ol","items":["**Unitary method:** one part $=\\dfrac{\\text{total}}{a+b}$; then multiply by $a$ and by $b$.","**Ratio table:** keep adding $a$ and $b$ until the total is reached.","**Algebra:** let the shares be $ax$ and $bx$, so $ax+bx=\\text{total}$."]},{"k":"p","text":"The same works for three-part ratios $a:b:c$ with $a+b+c$ parts."}],"figs":["w12-tape"]},{"title":"Combining ratios","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"If $A:B=2:3$ and $B:C=4:5$, make the $B$ parts equal (the LCM of 3 and 4 is 12): $A:B=8:12$ and $B:C=12:15$, so $A:B:C=8:12:15$."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Rates","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **rate** compares two quantities of **different kinds**, such as kilometres and hours. A **unit rate** gives the amount for **one** unit of the second quantity."},{"k":"table","head":["Rate","Example","Units"],"rows":[["speed","240 km in 4 h","60 km/h"],["pay rate","GH₵600 for 40 h","GH₵15 per hour"],["unit price","GH₵7.50 for 3 kg","GH₵2.50 per kg"],["fuel consumption","150 km on 10 L","15 km per litre"]]},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"Converting units of a rate","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Convert the top and bottom separately: $72\\text{ km/h}=\\dfrac{72\\,000\\text{ m}}{3600\\text{ s}}=20\\text{ m/s}$. In general, divide km/h by 3.6 to get m/s."}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Proportion","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **proportion** is an equation stating that two ratios or rates are equal:"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\frac ab=\\frac cd\\quad\\Longleftrightarrow\\quad ad=bc\\ \\ \\text{(cross-multiplication)}"},{"k":"fig","id":"w12-dnl","caption":"A double number line keeps the two quantities in proportion."}],"figs":["w12-dnl"]},{"title":"Direct and inverse proportion","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Direct and inverse proportion","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["$y$ is **directly proportional** to $x$ if $y=kx$ for a constant $k$. Doubling $x$ doubles $y$. The graph is a straight line through the origin.","$y$ is **inversely proportional** to $x$ if $y=\\dfrac kx$, that is $xy=k$. Doubling $x$ halves $y$. The graph is a curve that never meets the axes."]}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w12-prop","caption":"Direct proportion (left) and inverse proportion (right)."}],"figs":["w12-prop"]},{"title":"Scales and exchange rates","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **scale** $1:n$ means 1 unit on the map or model stands for $n$ of the same units in real life. Find (a) the ratio of boys to girls (b) the ratio of girls to the whole class (c) the percentage of girls."}],"steps":["(a) $30:20=3:2$ (divide by 10).","(b) The class has 50 students: $20:50=2:5$.","(c) $\\dfrac{2}{5}=40\\%$."],"answer":"(a) $3:2$ (b) $2:5$ (c) 40%","figs":[]},{"title":"Ratios from a population","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A town has 33 000 people, of whom 17 000 are female. Find the ratio of males to females, and of males to the whole population."}],"steps":["Males $=33\\,000-17\\,000=16\\,000$.","Males : females $=16\\,000:17\\,000=16:17$.","Males : whole $=16\\,000:33\\,000=16:33$."],"answer":"$16:17$ and $16:33$","figs":[]},{"title":"Sharing in a ratio three ways","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"In a class of 30 students, the ratio of boys to girls is $2:3$. How many boys and girls are there?"}],"steps":["**Unitary:** $2+3=5$ parts, so 1 part $=\\dfrac{30}{5}=6$. Boys $=2\\times6=12$, girls $=3\\times6=18$ (see the tape diagram in the notes).","**Ratio table:** $2:3,\\ 4:6,\\ 6:9,\\ \\dots,\\ 12:18$, where the total first reaches 30.","**Algebra:** $2x+3x=30$, so $x=6$: boys $2x=12$, girls $3x=18$."],"answer":"12 boys and 18 girls","figs":[]},{"title":"Combining ratios","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"$A:B=2:3$ and $B:C=4:5$. (a) Find $A:B:C$. (b) Share GH₵700 in this ratio."}],"steps":["(a) Make the $B$ parts equal to 12: $A:B=8:12$ and $B:C=12:15$, so $A:B:C=8:12:15$.","(b) Total parts $=8+12+15=35$, so 1 part $=\\dfrac{700}{35}=20$.","$A=160$, $B=240$, $C=300$. Check: $160+240+300=700$ ✓."],"answer":"(a) $8:12:15$ (b) GH₵160, GH₵240, GH₵300","figs":[]},{"title":"Rates and unit conversion","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) Alberta earns GH₵5000 for 24 hours of work. Find her hourly rate. (b) A car travels at 72 km/h. Write this in m/s."}],"steps":["(a) Rate $=\\dfrac{5000}{24}\\approx208.33$, that is GH₵208.33 per hour.","(b) $72$ km $=72\\,000$ m and 1 h $=3600$ s.","So $72\\text{ km/h}=\\dfrac{72\\,000}{3600}=20$ m/s."],"answer":"(a) GH₵208.33 per hour (b) 20 m/s","figs":[]},{"title":"Best buy","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A 500 g bag of rice costs GH₵12.50 and a 2 kg bag costs GH₵46. Which is better value?"}],"steps":["Compare the price of the same amount, say 100 g.","Small bag: $\\dfrac{12.50}{500}\\times100=$ GH₵2.50 per 100 g.","Large bag: $\\dfrac{46}{2000}\\times100=$ GH₵2.30 per 100 g.","The 2 kg bag is cheaper per gram, so it is the better buy (if you can use it all)."],"answer":"The 2 kg bag (GH₵2.30 per 100 g)","figs":[]},{"title":"Solving proportions","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) A dinner for 4 servings needs 2 cups of rice. How much rice is needed for 10 servings? (b) If 3 apples cost GH₵10.25, how much do 8 apples cost?"}],"steps":["(a) $\\dfrac{2}{4}=\\dfrac{x}{10}$, so $4x=20$ and $x=5$ cups (see the double number line in the notes).","(b) $\\dfrac{3}{10.25}=\\dfrac{8}{x}$, so $3x=8\\times10.25=82$.","$x=\\dfrac{82}{3}\\approx27.33$."],"answer":"(a) 5 cups (b) GH₵27.33","figs":[]},{"title":"Direct or inverse?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) 4 shirts cost GH₵60. Find the cost of 7 shirts. (b) 6 workers finish a job in 10 days. How long would 15 workers take, working at the same rate?"}],"steps":["(a) Cost is **directly** proportional to the number: $C=15n$ (GH₵15 per shirt). $C=15\\times7=$ GH₵105.","(b) More workers means **fewer** days: inverse proportion. The job takes $6\\times10=60$ worker-days.","With 15 workers: $\\dfrac{60}{15}=4$ days."],"answer":"(a) GH₵105 (b) 4 days","figs":[]},{"title":"Scales and exchange rates","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) A map has scale $1:100\\,000$. Two towns are 5 cm apart on it. How far apart are they? (b) A model car has scale $1:24$ and the real car is 4.8 m long. How long is the model? (c) At GH₵15.38 to 1 US dollar, how many cedis is 5275 US dollars?"}],"steps":["(a) Real distance $=5\\times100\\,000=500\\,000$ cm $=5$ km.","(b) Model length $=\\dfrac{4.8}{24}=0.2$ m $=20$ cm.","(c) $15.38\\times5275=$ GH₵81 129.50."],"answer":"(a) 5 km (b) 20 cm (c) GH₵81 129.50","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Ratio, rate and proportion","items":["Ratio: same units, $a:b$. Simplify by dividing by the HCF. Form $1:n$: divide by the first part.","Share in $a:b$: one part $=\\dfrac{\\text{total}}{a+b}$.","Rate: different units; unit rate $=$ amount per 1 unit.","Proportion: $\\dfrac ab=\\dfrac cd\\Leftrightarrow ad=bc$.","Direct: $y=kx$ (straight line through $O$). Inverse: $y=\\dfrac kx$ ($xy$ constant).","Scale $1:n$: real $=n\\times$ map."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"The ratio $45:30$ in simplest form is","options":["$3:2$","$2:3$","$9:6$","$15:10$"],"correct":0,"explain":"Divide by 15."},{"q":"50 cm : 2 m in simplest form is","options":["$1:4$","$25:1$","$50:2$","$1:40$"],"correct":0,"explain":"$50:200$."},{"q":"GH₵40 is shared in the ratio $3:5$. The larger share is","options":["GH₵25","GH₵15","GH₵24","GH₵20"],"correct":0,"explain":"One part is GH₵5."},{"q":"Which of these is a **rate**?","options":["60 km per hour","3 boys to 2 girls","$2:3:4$","20 cm to 1 m"],"correct":0,"explain":"It compares quantities of different kinds."},{"q":"90 km/h in m/s is","options":["25 m/s","90 m/s","324 m/s","15 m/s"],"correct":0,"explain":"$90\\div3.6$."},{"q":"If $\\dfrac{x}{6}=\\dfrac{10}{4}$, then $x=$","options":["15","2.4","20","12"],"correct":0,"explain":"$4x=60$."},{"q":"If $A:B=1:2$ and $B:C=3:4$, then $A:B:C=$","options":["$3:6:8$","$1:2:4$","$1:6:4$","$3:2:4$"],"correct":0,"explain":"Make $B$ equal to 6."},{"q":"8 taps fill a tank in 3 hours. How long would 6 taps take?","options":["4 hours","2.25 hours","5 hours","6 hours"],"correct":0,"explain":"$8\\times3=24$ tap-hours; $24\\div6=4$."},{"q":"On a map of scale $1:50\\,000$, 3 cm represents","options":["1.5 km","15 km","150 m","3 km"],"correct":0,"explain":"$150\\,000$ cm."},{"q":"The graph of a direct proportion is","options":["a straight line through the origin","a curve that never meets the axes","a horizontal line","a line with a negative gradient"],"correct":0,"explain":"$y=kx$."}],"exercise":[{"q":"The ratio of cats to dogs in a pet shop is $3:5$, and there are 40 animals. How many cats are there?","a":"15 cats"},{"q":"3 kg of apples cost GH₵7.50. What is the price per kg?","a":"GH₵2.50"},{"q":"A solution is 20% acid. How many millilitres of acid are in 250 mL of it?","a":"50 mL"},{"q":"A car travels 240 miles in 4 hours. Find its average speed in km/h (1 mile $=1.609$ km).","a":"$60\\times1.609\\approx96.5$ km/h"},{"q":"A recipe uses 2 cups of flour for every 3 eggs. How much flour is needed for 5 eggs?","a":"$\\tfrac{10}{3}=3\\tfrac13$ cups"},{"q":"Of 50 students surveyed, 13 are in Form 1, 14 in Form 2 and the rest in Form 3. Give a part-to-part and a part-to-whole ratio.","a":"e.g. Form 1 : Form 2 $=13:14$; Form 1 : all $=13:50$"},{"q":"A 20 m building casts a 12 m shadow. How tall is a tree that casts an 18 m shadow at the same time?","a":"$\\tfrac{20}{12}=\\tfrac{h}{18}$: $h=30$ m"},{"q":"A school has 1000 students and a student-to-teacher ratio of $25:1$. How many teachers are there?","a":"40"},{"q":"A farmer mixes fertiliser and water in the ratio $4:5$. How much water goes with 20 L of fertiliser?","a":"25 L"},{"q":"A taxi uses 10 L of fuel for 150 km. How much fuel is needed for 375 km?","a":"25 L"}],"theory":[{"q":"A table measures 1.2 m by 0.8 m. It is redesigned using the scale factor $5:3$ (new : old). Find the new dimensions, and compare the areas of the two tables.","steps":["Each length is multiplied by $\\tfrac53$: new length $=1.2\\times\\tfrac53=2$ m, new width $=0.8\\times\\tfrac53\\approx1.33$ m.","Old area $=1.2\\times0.8=0.96$ m². New area $=2\\times\\tfrac43=\\tfrac83\\approx2.67$ m².","Area ratio $=\\tfrac83:0.96=25:9$, which is $5^2:3^2$. When lengths are in the ratio $5:3$, areas are in the ratio $25:9$."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"A school with 1000 students keeps a student-to-teacher ratio of $25:1$. Next year 200 more students will enrol. How many extra teachers must be employed to keep the same ratio? What would the ratio be if no teachers were added?","steps":["Now: $\\dfrac{1000}{25}=40$ teachers. Next year: $\\dfrac{1200}{25}=48$ teachers, so **8 extra teachers** are needed.","If none were added: $1200:40=30:1$. Each teacher would then have 30 students instead of 25, a 20% heavier load."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"A car journey takes 2 hours at an average speed of 90 km/h. (a) Is time directly or inversely proportional to speed for a fixed journey? (b) How long would the journey take at 120 km/h? (c) What speed is needed to finish in 1 hour 30 minutes?","steps":["(a) Distance $=$ speed $\\times$ time is fixed ($90\\times2=180$ km), so speed $\\times$ time is constant: time is **inversely** proportional to speed.","(b) $t=\\dfrac{180}{120}=1.5$ h, that is 1 hour 30 minutes.","(c) The same as (b): $\\dfrac{180}{1.5}=120$ km/h. Increasing the speed by a third cuts the time by a quarter."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"A taxi driver's car covers 150 km on 10 litres of fuel. (a) Find the fuel consumption in km per litre and in litres per 100 km. (b) Fuel costs GH₵14 per litre. Find the fuel cost of a 375 km trip and the cost per kilometre.","steps":["(a) $\\dfrac{150}{10}=15$ km per litre; $\\ \\dfrac{10}{150}\\times100\\approx6.67$ litres per 100 km.","(b) Fuel needed $=\\dfrac{375}{15}=25$ L; cost $=25\\times14=$ GH₵350. Cost per km $=\\dfrac{350}{375}\\approx$ GH₵0.93 (or $\\tfrac{14}{15}$ of a cedi)."],"answer":"","model":null},{"q":"Increase GH₵240 in the ratio $5:4$, and decrease it in the ratio $3:4$. Explain how this links ratio to percentage change.","steps":["Increase in the ratio $5:4$: new $=240\\times\\tfrac54=$ GH₵300. That is a $25\\%$ increase, because $\\tfrac54=1.25$.","Decrease in the ratio $3:4$: new $=240\\times\\tfrac34=$ GH₵180. That is a $25\\%$ decrease, because $\\tfrac34=0.75$.","In general, changing a quantity in the ratio $m:n$ multiplies it by $\\tfrac mn$, the same as a percentage change with multiplier $\\tfrac mn$."],"answer":"","model":null}],"checklist":["I can tell part-to-part from part-to-whole ratios.","I can simplify ratios and write them in the form $1:n$.","I can share a quantity in a ratio and combine two ratios.","I can find unit rates, compare best buys and convert units of a rate.","I can solve proportions by cross-multiplying.","I can recognise and use direct and inverse proportion, scales and exchange
